answer:
**תשובה קצרה:** לפי הפוסקים המקובלים, לא. הקולא הידועה ביותר, של הרב עובדיה יוסף, מאפשרת להגיע לטבילה בליל היום ה-11 מתחילת הראייה. ספרדית שנוהגת כמותו וסופרת שבעה נקיים מלאים טובלת בלילה שאחרי היום ה-11. אשכנזייה טובלת בלילה שאחרי היום ה-12. לא מצאתי מקור ל"קולא של הבן איש חי" על שישה נקיים, ולכן אין לסמוך על שילוב כזה בלי שאלת רב.

## עיקרי הדברים
- **ספרדים:** הפסק טהרה ביום הרביעי, שבעה נקיים בימים 5–11, וטבילה בליל היום ה-11 ואילך.
- **אשכנזים:** לפי הרמ"א ממתינים חמישה ימים, כולל יום הראייה. מפסיקים טהרה ביום החמישי, סופרים ימים 6–12, וטובלים בלילה שאחרי היום ה-12.
- **שישה ימי נקיים:** לא מצאתי מקור לכך בבן איש חי. לפי השיטה המקובלת שבעה נקיים הם חובה, ולכן שילוב כזה אינו הלכה למעשה.
- **טבילה ביום ה-10:** אפשרית רק בשעת הדחק, ורק לפי הוראה פרטנית של רב.

## הדין והמקורות

**1. מקור שבעת הנקיים.** התורה אומרת: "וְאִשָּׁה כִּי תִהְיֶה זָבָה… וְאִם תִּטְהַר מִזּוֹבָהּ וְסָפְרָה לָּהּ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים" [Leviticus 15:25-28]. לנידה רגילה התורה קבעה שבעה ימים מהראייה [Leviticus 15:19]. חז"ל החמירו שכל בנות ישראל ינהגו כזבות ויספרו שבעה נקיים אחרי שפסקה מלראות [Niddah 66a]. לכן ארבעת או חמשת הימים הראשונים הם ימי ה"נידות", ושבעת הנקיים באים אחריהם ואינם נספרים בתוכם.

**2. הרמ"א (אשכנזים).** בסוף [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 196:11] כתב הרמ"א: "כל אשה שרואה אפי' כתם צריכה להמתין ה' ימים עם יום שראתה בו ותפסוק לעת ערב ותספור ז' נקיים… וכן נוהגין במדינות אלו ואין לשנות". לכן הימים 1–5 הם ימי נידות, ימים 6–12 הם שבעת הנקיים, והטבילה היא בליל אחריהם. זו המינימום לאשכנזים.

**3. המחבר (ספרדים).** בגוף [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 196:11] כתב המחבר, לגבי אשה ששמשה לפני שראתה, שאינה מתחילה לספור "עד יום ה' לשמושה". ממנו נובע שאין צורך לחכות חמישה ימים שלמים, ושדי בהפסק טהרה ביום הרביעי. הרמ"א הוסיף על כך יום נוסף. הרב עובדיה פסק כדעת המחבר, ולכן אצל ספרדים סופרים נקיים מהיום החמישי. זה מביא לטבילה בליל היום ה-11 ואילך. לא שלפתי כאן את דברי הרב עובדיה עצמם (ילקוט יוסף וטהרת הבית).

**4. שישה נקיים.** אם מקצרים את הנקיים לשישה, המסקנה המספרית נכונה (ימים 5–10, טבילה בליל היום ה-10 מהראייה), אבל אין לה בסיס הלכתי מקובל. חיפשתי בספריא ולא מצאתי קולא כזו בבן איש חי. הוא נהג בדרך כלל כדעת המחבר ולא כמקל מעבר לו. אם יש לך מקור מסוים, כדאי לבדוק אותו. לא ידוע לי על פוסק מרכזי שמתיר לחבר את שתי הקולות.

## האם יש מצב דחוק?
יש שאלות של שעת הדחק, כמו כלה לפני חתונה, עגונה, או מצב רפואי. בהן יש רבנים שדנים בשיקולי הקלה, למשל לפי הדין התורני שנידה סופרת שבעה ימים מהראייה. אלה הוראות פרטניות של רב שמכיר את כל הפרטים, ואינן שיטה כללית. גם אשה שראתה בלילה, או שהפסק הטהרה שלה נעשה בשעה מסוימת, עלולה לקבל חישוב שונה, וזו שאלה לרב.

## סיכום מעשי
- ספרדית: מינימום של 11 ימים עד הטבילה, ואם המנהג המשפחתי הוא כרמ"א, 12.
- אשכנזייה: מינימום של 12 ימים.
- חב"ד נוהגים כאשכנזים בעניין זה, ולא בדקתי שיש הבדל.
- הלכות נידה הן מהנושאים שחובה להתייעץ בהם עם רב או יועצת הלכה מוסמכת. אם יש צורך מיוחד לקצר, פני אל רב ושאלי אותו לפי הנסיבות שלך.

answer:
Die Tora verbietet Männern, den Bart mit einem Rasiermesser abzuscheren. Dahinter steht ein Verbot in Levitikus 19:27. Der Talmud und die Kodizes legen es so aus, dass es bestimmte Stellen des Bartes betrifft und eine bestimmte Art der Entfernung.

## Kernpunkte
- **Quelle:** Das Verbot steht in Levitikus 19:27 und gilt Männern.
- **Was verboten ist:** Das Verbot betrifft das „Zerstören“ (*haschchatat*) der Bartecken, traditionell mit einem Rasiermesser oder einem rasiermesserartigen Werkzeug.
- **Was nicht gemeint ist:** Nach der klassischen Halacha ist nicht jedes Kürzen des Bartes verboten.
- **Gemeindeunterschiede:** Beim Trimmen mit der Schere und beim elektrischen Rasierer gehen die Meinungen und Bräuche auseinander.

## Die Quelle in der Tora
> „לֹא תַקִּפוּ פְּאַת רֹאשְׁכֶם וְלֹא תַשְׁחִית אֵת פְּאַת זְקָנֶךָ“
> „Ihr sollt den Rand eures Kopfhaares nicht rundum abschneiden und die Ecke deines Bartes nicht zerstören.“ [Leviticus 19:27] (meine Übersetzung)

Wer den Bart so entfernt, übertritt nach dem Talmud ein Tora-Verbot. Der Traktat Makkot behandelt es: „פְּאַת זְקָנוֹ – סוֹף זְקָנוֹ, וְאֵיזֶהוּ סוֹף זְקָנוֹ – שִׁבּוֹלֶת זְקָנוֹ“. Das heißt: Die „Ecke“ des Bartes ist sein Ende, nämlich die „Ähre“ des Bartes, wo er wächst. [Makkot 20b]

## Was gilt als „Ecke“?
- Der Talmud nennt die Stellen nicht genau. Die Tradition, die Rambam und andere festhalten, spricht von fünf Stellen. Dazu gehören beide Seiten bei den Koteletten und am Kiefer sowie das Kinn.
- Die Details, also genaue Stellen, Schiur und Ausnahmen, stehen in [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 181](https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh,_Yoreh_De'ah.181). Dieses Kapitel behandelt auch die Pe'ot (Schläfenlocken). Ich habe dort nur den Anfang abgerufen, den Rest nenne ich ohne Seifnummern.

## Rasiermesser, Schere, Elektrorasierer
- **Rasiermesser:** Es ist eindeutig verboten, wenn es die Haare an der Haut abschneidet.
- **Schere:** Eine Schere, die wie ein Rasiermesser dicht an der Haut schneidet, gilt als verboten. Ein Kürzen mit deutlichem Abstand ist nach der Grundhalacha erlaubt.
- **Elektrorasierer:** Hier gibt es keine einheitliche Praxis.
  - Manche Poskim erlauben Geräte, die nach Art einer Schere arbeiten, besonders solche mit Schutzgitter. Dazu gehört Rav Moshe Feinstein.
  - Andere verbieten sie, weil das Ergebnis dem Rasieren gleicht. Das gilt unter anderem in vielen chassidischen Kreisen.
  - Wenn du einen Elektrorasierer benutzen willst, frag deinen Rabbiner, welches Gerät und welche Einstellung er erlaubt.

## Unterschiede nach Gemeinde
- **Aschkenasim:** Viele folgen der Linie, dass eine Schere mit Abstand und bestimmte Rasierer erlaubt sein können. Manche gehen trotzdem strenger vor.
- **Sefardim:** Hier gilt die Linie des Mechaber, bei den Einzelfragen mit Unterschieden je nach Posek.
- **Chabad und Kabbalisten:** Sie lassen den Bart wachsen und kürzen ihn nicht. Das beruht auf dem Zohar und dem Ari (R. Yitzchak Luria), die den Bart als Quelle von Segen und Gnade sehen. Dabei handelt es sich um eine Stringenz (*chumra*), nicht um das Grundgesetz.

## Der Sinn des Gebots
Die Tora nennt keinen Grund für dieses Gebot (*chok*). Deshalb gibt es mehrere Erklärungen:
- **Abgrenzung von heidnischen Bräuchen:** Der Rambam erklärt das Verbot im Zusammenhang mit götzendienerischen Ritualen. [Mishneh Torah, Idolatry 12](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishneh_Torah,_Foreign_Worship_and_Customs_of_the_Nations.12)
- **Würde und Männlichkeit:** Der Bart gilt als Zierde des Mannes.
- **Kabbala:** Die Bartlocken haben nach dieser Lehre eine geistige Bedeutung für den Fluss von Gnade (die „13 Maßen des Bartes“).

## Praktisch
- Das Verbot gilt für Männer.
- Wenn du bisher rasiert hast und dich jetzt fragst, was du tun sollst, hilft ein Gespräch mit einem Rabbiner. Bei deinem Beruf oder deinen Umständen kann es Besonderheiten geben.
- Das gilt auch für die Frage, welcher Rasierer und welche Technik in deiner Gemeinde üblich ist.

Bitte wende dich für deinen persönlichen Fall an deinen Rabbiner.

answer:
**Respuesta breve:** La postura histórica del movimiento Masorti (Conservador fuera de Israel) permite conducir en Shabbat solo para ir a la sinagoga. Es una excepción basada en una *teshuvá* (responsa) del Comité de Ley y Normas Judías (CJLS) de 1950. Viajar en Shabbat por ocio, compras o negocios sigue desaconsejado o prohibido para la mayoría de las autoridades masortíes. La halajá ortodoxa, en cambio, prohíbe viajar en vehículo motorizado en Shabbat.

## Puntos clave
- La responsa de 1950 (Adler, Agus y Friedman) permitió conducir a la sinagoga cuando la distancia lo hace necesario, para no dejar de asistir a la comunidad y a la oración.
- Esa permisión es limitada: no autoriza los viajes recreativos ni comerciales.
- Los líderes masortíes difieren entre sí. Muchos dicen que la excepción solo vale para quien vive lejos de una sinagoga, y en Israel la práctica masortí suele ser más estricta.
- Los rabinos del movimiento no coinciden en la razón del permiso, y no todos lo aceptan.
- La halajá ortodoxa, ya sea ashkenazí, sefardí o jabad, prohíbe conducir en Shabbat.

## La posición masortí/conservadora
- **La responsa de 1950.** El CJLS aprobó una responsa que sostiene que conducir a la sinagoga está permitido. Argumenta que la combustión de un motor no equivale a la "melajá" bíblica de encender fuego. Argumenta también que el valor de la oración comunitaria y de la vida de la comunidad justifica el permiso.
- **Otras opiniones dentro del movimiento.** Hubo responsas y voces disidentes, y el movimiento nunca fue uniforme. Rabinos como David Golinkin, del movimiento Masorti en Israel, restringen el permiso a quien no tiene sinagoga a distancia de caminata. Aun así, subrayan que el ideal es vivir cerca de la sinagoga y caminar a ella.
- **Limitación.** Nada de esto convierte el viaje en Shabbat en algo libre. Las autoridades masortíes hablan de la sinagoga como excepción, no de viajar por placer.
- Esto lo cito de memoria sobre la historia del movimiento y no he consultado las responsas originales. Conviene que verifique el texto exacto con un rabino masortí o en el sitio del CJLS.

## La base en las fuentes tradicionales
- La Torá dice: "Quedaos cada uno en su lugar, que nadie salga de su lugar en el séptimo día" ([Exodus 16:29](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus%2016:29)).
- También dice: "No encenderéis fuego en ninguna de vuestras moradas en el día de Shabbat" ([Exodus 35:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus%2035:3)).
- Los sabios limitaron el desplazamiento mediante el *tejum Shabbat* (límite de unos 2000 codos fuera de la ciudad). Su fuente principal es el tratado [Eruvin](https://www.sefaria.org/Eruvin).

## La posición ortodoxa
- La mayoría de los *poskim* ortodoxos ven en el motor de combustión un encendido continuo de fuego, o bien otras prohibiciones: *boné* (construir), *maké be-patish* (golpe final) y el uso de electricidad. Por eso es un motivo central de la prohibición, entre otros.
- Además, viajar en vehículo suele exceder el *tejum*, y a menudo implica pedir a un no judío que lo haga o cargar objetos.
- Esta postura es común a ashkenazíes, sefardíes y jabad. Hay variaciones menores de detalle, pero no sobre conducir.
- Excepción general: en caso de *pikuaj nefesh* (peligro de vida) se permite todo lo necesario, incluso viajar, tanto en la visión ortodoxa como en la masortí.

Para su caso personal, consulte a su rabino, ya sea de su comunidad masortí o de la ortodoxa, según la que siga.

answer:
**Resposta curta:** O gentio não tem obrigação de sentar na sucá. Segundo a Torá, a mitzvá é para Israel. Mesmo assim, a maioria das fontes permite que um gentio que queira sentar na sucá o faça de forma voluntária. Isso vale desde que ele não crie para si uma "religião nova" nem trate o ato como obrigação.

## Pontos principais
- A fonte do versículo é restrita a Israel: "כׇּל־הָאֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשְׁבוּ בַּסֻּכֹּת" ("todo cidadão em Israel habitará em cabanas") [Leviticus 23:42].
- O não judeu é obrigado às sete leis de Noé. As demais mitzvot não são obrigação dele.
- O Rambam permite que o filho de Noé cumpra outras mitzvot para receber recompensa, desde que as faça como a halachá exige [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:10].
- O Rambam proíbe criar rituais novos ou instituir um "dia sagrado" próprio [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:9].
- Há divergência entre os poskim sobre o alcance dessa permissão. Por isso, a prática concreta deve ser perguntada a um rabino.

## Fontes e explicação

**1. Obrigação.** O versículo diz "ezrach b'Yisrael". A tradição talmúdica lê nele apenas o judeu, e é por isso que o gentio não está obrigado. Não consegui abrir o Talmud (Sucá 28b) nesta consulta, então cito só o princípio geral e não o texto.

**2. Pode fazer de forma voluntária?** O Rambam escreve: "בֶּן נֹחַ שֶׁרָצָה לַעֲשׂוֹת מִצְוָה מִשְּׁאָר מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה כְּדֵי לְקַבֵּל שָׂכָר. אֵין מוֹנְעִין אוֹתוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ כְּהִלְכָתָהּ". Em tradução: o filho de Noé que quer cumprir uma das outras mitzvot da Torá para receber recompensa não é impedido, desde que a cumpra conforme a lei [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:10]. Ele dá como exemplo a oferta de holocausto e a tzedacá. Pela lógica do Rambam, sentar na sucá se encaixa nesse princípio.

**3. O limite.** No halacha anterior, o Rambam afirma que "não deixam [os gentios] inovar uma religião nem fazer mitzvot para si por sua própria opinião". Ou seja, ou se tornam convertidos, ou permanecem na sua própria lei "sem acrescentar nem diminuir" [Mishneh Torah, Kings and Wars 10:9]. Ele dá como exemplos estudar Torá de forma ampla e guardar um descanso como Shabat ou criar uma festa.

Há então uma tensão entre os dois halachot. Muitos comentaristas a resolvem assim:
- Se o gentio cumpre a mitzvá como um ato isolado, como um judeu cumpriria, isso é permitido.
- Se ele institui uma festa própria ou uma prática religiosa nova, isso é proibido.

Esta é minha explicação do assunto, não uma citação de uma fonte específica.

**4. Na prática.**
- Um gentio pode ser convidado para uma refeição na sucá, e isso é comum.
- Quem é gentio e quer fazer a mitzvá "como mitzvá" deve consultar um rabino. Uma dúvida frequente é se ele pode recitar a bênção *leshev basucá*, que fala em "nos santificou com Suas mitzvot". Em geral, a bênção não é recitada por quem não é judeu.
- Se a pessoa está considerando a conversão, essa é uma conversa à parte, com um beit din reconhecido.

Consulte seu rabino para o seu caso pessoal.

answer:
**Réponse directe :** sur une tomate, on dit *Boré péri haadama* (בורא פרי האדמה). La tomate pousse sur une plante annuelle, pas sur un arbre. Elle suit donc la règle des produits de la terre.

## Points essentiels
- La bénédiction de la tomate est *haadama*, qu'elle soit crue, en salade ou en tranches.
- On ne dit pas *haêts*, parce que la tomate ne pousse pas sur un arbre.
- Cuite ou en sauce, elle reste *haadama*.
- Après avoir mangé, on ne dit pas de bénédiction finale (*boré nefashot*) si on n'a mangé que quelques tomates, car la quantité requise n'est pas atteinte.

## Source et explication

**La règle de base.** Le Choulhan Aroukh pose le principe : « Sur les fruits de la terre, on dit *Boré péri haadama* » (עַל פֵּרוֹת הָאָרֶץ מְבָרֵךְ בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה). [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 203:1]. Le Talmud en donne l'origine dans [Berakhot 35a], où la bénédiction *haêts* est réservée aux fruits d'un arbre.

**Pourquoi *haadama* pour la tomate.** Un arbre, au sens de la halakha, est une plante dont le tronc subsiste d'une année à l'autre et qui produit des fruits sur les mêmes branches. La tomate vient d'un plant herbacé qu'on sème chaque année. C'est donc un légume du sol, comme le concombre ou le poivron.

**Cuite ou transformée.** Pour les légumes, la cuisson ne change en général pas la bénédiction, qui reste *haadama*. C'est le cas du jus de tomate, de la sauce et du ketchup. S'ils sont mangés avec du pain pendant un repas, ils sont couverts par la bénédiction *hamotsi* et ne demandent pas de bénédiction à part.

**Cas particulier.** Si la tomate est mangée au cours d'un repas avec pain, elle est elle aussi couverte par *hamotsi*. Si on la mange seule comme dessert ou en dehors du repas, on dit *haadama*.

*Remarque :* je n'ai récupéré dans cette réponse que le texte du Choulhan Aroukh. Les détails sur la cuisson et les quantités sont des règles bien connues, que je n'ai pas vérifiées ici dans les sources.

answer:
**Respuesta corta:** No. Encender fuego en Shabat está prohibido por la Torá. Sí es una mitzvá encender las velas de Shabat *antes* de que empiece el día. La excepción es el peligro de vida (*pikuaj nefesh*), que permite hacer lo necesario. No pude consultar Sefaria en este momento (error del servidor), así que parafraseo las fuentes y no cito textos literales.

## Puntos clave
- La Torá prohíbe encender fuego en Shabat: [Exodus 35:3].
- Es una de las 39 *melajot* (labores prohibidas). Incluye encender una llama y también pasar la llama de una vela a otra.
- Las velas de Shabat se encienden antes del atardecer, y esa es una mitzvá.
- Por peligro de vida, o para salvar a alguien, se permite e incluso se exige encender fuego.
- Hay otras dudas frecuentes: luz eléctrica, estufa, o Yom Tov. Cada una tiene reglas distintas.

## La fuente
La Torá dice: "No encenderán fuego en ninguna de sus moradas en el día de Shabat" [Exodus 35:3]. Esta es mi traducción, parafraseada. La Mishná enumera la *hav'arah* (encender) entre las 39 labores prohibidas. Rambam la desarrolla en [Mishneh Torah, Sabbath 12], y el Shulchan Aruj trata la mayoría de estas leyes en Oraj Jayim, simanim 261 en adelante, y 273 y siguientes (no pude verificar los números exactos de seif).

## Qué incluye en la práctica
- **Encender un fósforo, un encendedor o una estufa de gas** está prohibido.
- **Pasar fuego de una vela a otra** también está prohibido en Shabat. Es encender una llama nueva.
- **Apagar una llama** también está prohibido, aunque por otra categoría (*kibui*).
- **Electricidad:** los poskim ortodoxos prohíben encender y apagar luces o aparatos eléctricos en Shabat. Hay diferencias en el motivo (por ejemplo, la Torá o un decreto rabínico), pero el resultado práctico es el mismo para casi todos. No hay diferencia práctica entre ashkenazíes, sefardíes y jabad en este punto.

## Lo que sí se puede y se debe hacer
- **Encender las velas de Shabat** antes de que empiece Shabat. Es costumbre hacerlo unos 18 minutos antes del atardecer, y en Jerusalem 40. Para los horarios de tu ciudad puedo usar el calendario si me dices dónde estás.
- **Dejar prendida una llama** (por ejemplo, el fuego de la estufa o una vela de 24 horas) desde antes de Shabat. Se puede usar sin volver a encenderla, según las reglas de *jazaká* (mantener calor y cocción).
- **Yom Tov** es diferente. Se permite *pasar* una llama ya existente para cocinar o para necesidades de la fiesta, pero no encender fuego nuevo. En Shabat esto no vale.

## Peligro de vida
Si hay un enfermo en peligro, frío extremo, o una emergencia, se permite encender fuego e incluso se debe, sin dudar. "Se vivirá por ellas" (*vajai bahem*, [Leviticus 18:5]) es el principio que los Sabios aplican en [Yoma 85b]. No hay que preguntar primero si hay peligro real. Se actúa, y después se consulta.

Si tu pregunta es sobre un caso concreto, por ejemplo calefacción en invierno, un enfermo, un niño o un temporizador, cuéntamelo y lo vemos. Para tu situación personal, consulta con tu rabino.

answer:
Oui. Selon la halakha, le cunnilingus est en principe permis entre mari et femme, y compris pour les séfarades. Cela vaut à deux conditions: les deux conjoints y consentent, et on respecte les règles de *niddah* (pureté familiale). Une réserve existe dans la tradition kabbalistique, que je détaille plus bas.

Les outils de consultation des sources ont échoué à l'instant (erreur 429). Je m'appuie donc sur ma connaissance des textes, sans citer de formulations exactes. Je vous invite à vérifier les références.

## Points clés
- Le principe talmudique est que le mari peut agir avec son épouse comme il le désire, à condition qu'elle consente.
- Le Rambam et le Shulchan Aroukh (rite séfarade) tranchent dans ce sens.
- Les restrictions sérieuses portent sur l'émission de semence en vain, et sur la période de *niddah*.
- Le Zohar et le Ben Ish Haï conseillent la retenue et la sainteté, mais ce sont des recommandations, pas une interdiction.
- Il n'existe pas de différence de fond entre séfarades et ashkénazes sur ce point.

## Les sources
**Talmud.** Dans [Nedarim 20b], Rabbi Yohanan ben Dahabaï rapporte une opinion d'après laquelle certains comportements conjugaux auraient des conséquences sur les enfants. Les sages la rejettent: "Ce n'est pas comme il dit, mais la halakha est que l'homme fait avec sa femme ce qu'il veut." Le Talmud compare cela à de la viande qui vient de la boucherie: on peut la manger rôtie, bouillie, etc. Le passage met en garde contre la contrainte et contre les comportements indécents ou irrespectueux, et il insiste sur le consentement de la femme.

**Rambam.** Dans [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9], il écrit que l'homme peut avoir avec sa femme toute relation qu'il désire, y compris par l'union naturelle ou non. Il ajoute qu'il est pieux de ne pas faire preuve de légèreté, et de se sanctifier au moment de l'union. Il précise que l'émission de semence en vain est interdite.

**Shulchan Aroukh.** Dans [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2], le Mehaber (R. Yossef Karo, suivi par les séfarades) reprend cette position. Il rappelle qu'on ne doit pas émettre de semence en vain, et que la retenue est préférable. Le Rema (ashkénaze) n'y contredit pas sur le principe.

## Nuances pour les séfarades
- **Semence en vain.** Le cunnilingus ne pose pas ce problème en lui-même. Il faut simplement veiller à ne pas aboutir à une émission de semence en dehors de l'union.
- **Niddah.** Pendant la période d'impureté (jusqu'au *mikvé*), tout contact intime est interdit, ainsi que tout rapport entre les époux. Ce cas relève d'un rav.
- **Zohar et Kabbale.** Les kabbalistes, dont le Ben Ish Haï dans la tradition séfarade irakienne, recommandent de sanctifier l'union et de limiter les comportements trop charnels. Certains décisionnaires sépharades contemporains, comme le Rav Ovadia Yossef, ont aussi exprimé une préférence pour la retenue. Je n'ai pas pu vérifier leurs formulations précises ici, donc je m'abstiens de les citer.
- **Hygiène et respect.** Le consentement libre, sans pression, est une condition essentielle.

## Recommandation
Chaque couple a sa situation propre, et plusieurs détails dépendent de la coutume locale et de la sensibilité de chacun. Consultez un rabbin compétent, de préférence séfarade, pour votre cas personnel. Beaucoup de rabbanim répondent à ces questions en toute discrétion.

**Non. Dans le judaïsme, la Torah n'interdit pas le mariage entre cousins germains.** Les unions interdites (*arayot*) sont énumérées de façon limitative en [Leviticus 18](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.18) et [Leviticus 20](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.20). (Les outils de consultation m'ont renvoyé une erreur lors de ma recherche. Je cite donc les sources de mémoire, sans citation littérale.)

## Points clés
- Le mariage entre cousins germains n'est pas interdit par la Torah, car il n'apparaît pas dans la liste des relations interdites de Lévitique 18 et 20.
- La Torah et le Talmud rapportent des mariages entre cousins, et le Talmud encourage même les unions au sein de la famille.
- Les oncles et tantes sont interdits, mais pas les cousins. Il ne faut pas confondre les deux.
- Il n'existe pas de différence de principe entre Ashkénazes, Séfarades et ʿHabad sur ce point.
- Il peut y avoir une réserve médicale ou génétique, qui relève d'une consultation médicale et rabbinique.

## Ce que dit la Torah
- **Lévitique 18** interdit les relations avec la mère, la sœur, la fille, la petite-fille, la tante paternelle ou maternelle, la belle-fille, la belle-sœur, etc. Les cousins sont absents de la liste. Selon le principe d'interprétation, ce qui n'est pas énuméré n'est pas interdit.
- **Exemples bibliques :**
  - Yaʿakov a épousé Rachel et Léa, ses cousines germaines, filles de son oncle Lavan.
  - Yitzhak a épousé Rivka, la petite-fille du frère de son père Avraham.
  - Les filles de Tselofhad se sont mmariées avec les fils de leurs oncles paternels ([Numbers 36:11](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.36.11)). Cela se faisait dans le cadre de la règle de l'héritage tribal.

## Ce que dit le Talmud
Le Talmud ([Yevamot 62b](https://www.sefaria.org/Yevamot.62b)) loue celui qui « aime ses proches » et « épouse la fille de sa sœur ». Ce dernier cas est une nièce, qui n'est pas interdite en droit juif, contrairement à la tante. Les cousins étaient donc d'autant moins problématiques. Le Choulkhan Aroukh ([Even HaEzer, siman 2](https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh,_Even_HaEzer.2)) reprend cette approche favorable au mariage dans la famille.

## Pratique
- **Ashkénazes, Séfarades et ʿHabad :** le mariage entre cousins germains est permis. Beaucoup de communautés l'ont pratiqué, notamment des communautés séfarades et orientales.
- **Réserve actuelle :** certaines familles et certains rabbins recommandent un conseil génétique, surtout lorsqu'il y a déjà des maladies héréditaires. Les unions répétées dans une même famille augmentent ce risque. Ce n'est pas une interdiction de la Torah, mais une prudence, car la Torah demande de protéger la santé ([Deuteronomy 4:15](https://www.sefaria.org/Deuteronomy.4.15)).
- **Ne pas confondre :** l'oncle et la tante, ainsi que la belle-mère ou la belle-fille, sont interdits. Les cousins ne le sont pas.

Pour votre situation personnelle, consultez votre rabbin.

answer:
Sinks didn't invent new Shabbat laws. They let us keep old ones more easily. A sink carries water away through a pipe, so you avoid several problems that arise when you pour liquids out by hand. The details of using a sink on Shabbat and Yom Tov still depend on your community's practice. I retrieved only a few of the sources below. Where I cite a work without a reference number, I am relying on my own knowledge of it.

## Key Takeaways
- The ancestor of the sink is the *kiyor* (copper laver) in the Mishkan, which the *kohanim* used to wash their hands and feet before serving.
- A drain moves water out of the house, so there is no pouring onto soil or plants and no pouring out into the street.
- Washing dishes on Shabbat and Yom Tov is permitted for use during that day, but sponges, soap, and food scraps need care.
- Hot water, and removing scraps from the strainer, are the main areas where halachic caution applies.
- Hand-washing at the sink connects the home to the Temple service.

## The sink in the Torah: the *kiyor*
The Torah commands: "Make a laver of copper and a stand of copper for it, for washing… Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet [in water drawn] from it… that they may not die" [Exodus 30:17-21]. The Mishnah in Yoma describes how the Kohen Gadol's Temple was improved. Ben Katin added spigots to the *kiyor*, so that more than one *kohen* could wash at once. I am citing that from memory.

Exodus 38:8 says the laver was made from the mirrors of the women who gathered at the Tent. Rashi, citing the Midrash, explains that these were mirrors the women had used to beautify themselves for their husbands. Moses hesitated to accept them, but God told him they were dearer to Him than anything else. The vessel of purification came from instruments of marital love and hope.

## Halachic issues a sink helps with
These are my own explanations of how the sources apply to a sink. They are not direct quotations.

1. **Disposing of water on Shabbat.** Without plumbing, dirty water has to be thrown out somewhere. Pouring it onto soil raises concerns about watering plants. Pouring it into the street raises concerns about carrying into the public domain. A drain sends the water into the pipe and avoids both. Compare the discussion of vegetation and roots on Shabbat [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 336:6].
2. **Washing dishes.** The code has a section on rinsing and washing vessels on Shabbat [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 323]. The general rule is that you may wash only what you need for use on Shabbat itself. On Yom Tov the rules are similar, and are laid out in Orach Chayim 503. Many authorities allow washing dishes after the last meal of Shabbat only if you will use them again that Shabbat.
3. **Sponges and soap.** Use non-absorbent scouring pads so you don't squeeze out water (the *sechitah* concern). Use liquid soap that has been thinned, not thick gel or bar soap, because of the concern of *memarei'ach* (smoothing a surface). Ashkenazim generally follow the Mishnah Berurah on this. Sephardim often follow the Mechaber with Rav Ovadia Yosef's rulings. Details differ, so ask your rabbi.
4. **Food scraps and *borer*.** Don't use a strainer to separate food from water. Leave the scraps for after Shabbat, or remove them together with some of the water.
5. **Hot water.** Water from a boiler or an electric heater raises the issues of cooking and *gerama*, because opening the tap draws in fresh cold water that then gets heated. Many people use only cold water on Shabbat, or use a heater with a halachic setup. This is an area for a rabbi's guidance.
6. **Hand-washing (*netilat yadayim*).** A sink makes it easy to wash hands from a vessel before bread, on Shabbat and on weekdays. The *kiyor* itself was an act of preparation for service.

## Inspiring Torah
- **The home as a Temple.** The Talmud says that after the Temple's destruction, a person's table atones, as the altar once did [Berakhot 55a]. In the same way, the kitchen sink recalls the *kiyor*. Washing before eating, and rinsing the dishes, extends the Temple's holiness into ordinary life.
- **Washing hands as service.** The prophet Elisha is introduced as the one "who poured water on the hands of Elijah" [2 Kings 3:11]. Our tradition treats pouring water for a teacher as a sign of devotion, and the sink gives us a daily chance to do the same for ourselves.
- **Mirrors and purification.** The *kiyor* was made of the women's mirrors. The Sages see in this a lesson about self-examination: before serving, you look at yourself, then you wash.
- **The drain as letting go.** This is my own reflection, not a classical source. Water that has done its work leaves through the drain. Letting go of what no longer serves us is part of *teshuvah* (repentance).

Consult your rabbi for your personal situation, especially on hot water, soap, and sponge use on Shabbat and Yom Tov.

answer:
**Short answer:** Chazal never discuss a kitchen sink as we know it, so there are no sources on "inventions of sinks" in that sense. The closest ancient "sink" is the *kiyor* (the Temple washbasin). The Mishnah credits an "invention" that solved a real problem for it. The Shabbat and Yom Tov issues that modern sinks raise come from later halachic literature built on Talmudic principles. I'm giving those from memory without chapter numbers, because the Sefaria tool failed (rate-limited) when I tried to pull the texts.

## Key Takeaways
- The *kiyor* is the biblical "sink" ([Exodus 30:17-21](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus%2030:17-21)). Its washing was required before Temple service.
- In the Mishnah (Yoma 3:10, which I believe is the source), Ben Katin added spigots and a mechanism that lowered the kiyor into a well. This kept its water from becoming invalid overnight.
- Hand-washing (*netilat yadayim*) is the Talmud's main "sink" topic, and it needs a vessel and a person's force. A modern tap and basin raise questions in that area.
- For Shabbat, a sink mostly raises questions about draining, dishes, sponges, and hot water. These were settled by later authorities using Talmudic categories.

## 1. The kiyor: the original "sink"
- **Source.** The Torah commands a copper basin for Aaron and his sons to wash their hands and feet before service ([Exodus 30:17-21](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus%2030:17-21)).
- **The Mishnah's "invention."** As I recall [Mishnah Yoma 3:10](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishnah_Yoma.3.10), Ben Katin made twelve spigots for the kiyor, where before it had two. He also made a mechanism (*mukhni*) so the kiyor could be sunk into the well at night. The Gemara ([Yoma 37a](https://www.sefaria.org/Yoma.37a)) discusses why. Water left standing overnight (*linah*) is invalid for sanctifying the hands and feet. Sinking the kiyor into a well kept its water attached to a valid source.
- **Insight.** The word "sink" fits literally here, since the basin was lowered into the ground. The point is that holiness depends on freshness and renewal. Water that has "stayed overnight" cannot serve. The Mishnah says Ben Katin's improvement was praised, and the Gemara reads it as a way to make the service easier for more *kohanim* at once.
- **Insight on materials.** The Torah says the kiyor was made from the mirrors of the women who gathered at the Tent of Meeting ([Exodus 38:8](https://www.sefaria.org/Exodus%2038:8)). Rashi cites the midrash that Moshe was at first reluctant to accept them, and God told him to. The idea is that what was used for vanity became the vessel for purity.

## 2. Netilat yadayim: the everyday sink
- **Sources.** The Talmud's main discussions are in [Berakhot 60b](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.60b) (the blessing on waking), [Sotah 4b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.4b) and [Chullin 106a](https://www.sefaria.org/Chullin.106a). Washing before bread requires a *kli* (vessel), and the water must be poured with human force (*koach gavra*).
- **What the sink solves.** A sink provides a place to pour the water away and a basin to catch it. A tap with running water raises the question of whether it counts as a vessel and as human force. Later authorities discuss this at length. One approach is to fill a cup from the tap and pour from the cup.

## 3. Sinks on Shabbat and Yom Tov
Common issues that later poskim derive from Talmudic categories (without exact references here):
- **Draining water.** Pouring liquid onto the ground is fine, and a sink drain is treated similarly. Poskim discuss food particles and whether blocking a drain is a problem.
- **Washing dishes.** This is allowed if you need the dishes for Shabbat itself. Poskim also restrict using a sponge that absorbs water, because of the prohibition on wringing (*sechitah*), and they recommend a plastic scrubber. Soap raises the issue of making a paste or smearing (*memare'ach*). Liquid soap is the accepted solution.
- **Hot water.** A tap connected to a water heater runs into the principle of cooking (*bishul*) and the prohibition on cooking in a vessel that is *kli rishon*. A question also arises when cold water enters a hot heater and heats up. This is why many people shut off the heater before Shabbat.
- **Yom Tov.** Cooking is permitted for food, but washing dishes on Yom Tov is limited to what is needed for the holiday.
- **Bathing.** For context, see [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 326:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh,_Orach_Chayim.326.1). It forbids washing the entire body on Shabbat, even in water heated before Shabbat. The Mechaber allows the face, hands and feet. The Rema notes that the prohibition covers water heated by fire, and that naturally hot springs like Tiberias are permitted when the water is in the ground.

## Next steps
If you give me a specific angle, I can retry the tool and pull exact texts. I could look at the Gemara in Yoma on the kiyor, the Shabbat sources on draining and sponges, or the modern poskim on taps. As with any practical question, consult your rabbi for your own kitchen and situation.

answer:
**Short answer:** An ingredient-scanning app can help you screen products, but it can't make a product "kosher permissible" by itself. A product's ingredient list doesn't show everything that matters for kashrut. A reliable *hechsher* (kosher certification) is what you actually rely on, so use the app as an aid and not as the final authority. I'm assuming you're asking whether you may rely on such an app. If you meant using a phone on Shabbat, that's a separate question.

## Key Takeaways
- An ingredient list can show that something is *not* kosher, but it often can't show that something *is* kosher.
- Many kashrut issues never appear on a label: equipment, processing aids, flavors, and Jewish supervision of certain foods.
- Halacha lets you rely on a source only if it is trustworthy and knowledgeable, and an app's reliability depends on who runs it and how it is updated.
- The safest use is to match products against kosher certification (the hechsher symbol) and to treat "no problem found" as less certain than "problem found."
- For a real decision, especially after the fact, ask your rabbi.

## Why a photo of the ingredients isn't enough

**1. Things the label doesn't list.**
- Shared equipment: a product can have fully kosher ingredients but be made on equipment also used for non-kosher items.
- Processing aids and "natural flavors": suppliers often don't disclose these, and they may be animal- or grape-derived.
- Some foods need Jewish involvement or supervision no matter what the ingredients are. These include wine and grape products, certain cheeses, and food cooked by a non-Jew (*bishul akum*). Some communities also require *pas Yisrael* (bread baked by a Jew). A photo of the ingredients can't show any of this.
- Insects, in produce and other foods, and meat and dairy status (*pareve* labeling) also need supervision.

**2. The halachic principle of trusting a source.**
Halacha doesn't let you rely on someone whose reliability isn't established. For example: "החשוד לדבר איסור אין לסמוך עליו בדברים הנאכלים" ("One who is suspected of eating forbidden things may not be relied on regarding foods") [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 119:1]. The Rema adds that some authorities say that even someone who is merely not known to be reliable in kashrut shouldn't be relied on for wine or other items of concern.

This doesn't apply to an app directly. The same logic does carry over, though: you may rely on a source only if you have reason to trust its knowledge and reliability. An app that uses image recognition or a database has no accountability or rabbinic supervision unless it is run by a recognized kashrut organization.

**3. Small amounts can still matter.**
In some cases a tiny amount of a forbidden ingredient is nullified if the permitted food is sixty times as much (*bittul b'shishim*) [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 98:1]. But that rule depends on the details of the case, including what the ingredient is and how it got there. Manufacturers also use it to decide what to list, so an app can't safely apply it to a label.

## Practical approach
- **Best:** Look for a reliable hechsher you trust. Different communities rely on different certifications, so ask your rabbi which ones to accept.
- **Acceptable use of an app:** Use it to flag obvious problems, such as gelatin, carmine, or animal-derived ingredients. Also use it to look up whether a product carries a recognized hechsher, ideally from an app run by a kashrut agency.
- **Not recommended:** Treating "the app found nothing wrong" as proof that an uncertified product is kosher.
- **Community differences:** Ashkenazim, Sephardim, and Chabad can differ on particular issues, such as *pas Yisrael*, *chalav Yisrael*, and which hechsherim they accept. An app should be used with your own community's standards.

This is a general overview and not a ruling for your situation. Please consult your rabbi.

answer:
**Short answer:** Between a husband and wife, anal intercourse is a disputed and sensitive question in halacha. It is not treated like the Torah's prohibition on male-male intercourse. Many authorities permit it in principle, but only if there is no emission of seed there. Others discourage it strongly or forbid it. I couldn't load the texts from Sefaria just now, so I'm giving the sources by name and paraphrasing them. Please check the exact wording yourself.

## Key Takeaways
- The Torah's explicit prohibition on anal intercourse is for two men [Leviticus 18:22].
- The Talmud says a husband may do what he wishes with his wife, using the image of a person who eats meat from the market. This is the basis for leniency [Nedarim 20b].
- The Rambam permits whatever the couple wish, provided there is no wasting of seed [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9]. The Shulchan Arukh follows him, and the Rema adds cautions [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2].
- The main objection is *hotza'at zera levatalah* (wasting seed). Many poskim therefore forbid it or limit it heavily, and some mystical sources are stricter still.
- Practice varies by community and by posek, so this is a question for a rabbi.

## The sources

**1. Talmud.** *Nedarim* 20b cites Rabbi Yochanan ben Dahavai's teachings, which the Sages reject. The Sages say that the halacha is not like him, and that a person may do whatever he wishes with his wife. They compare it to eating meat from the market: he may eat it salted, roasted, cooked, or boiled. This is the foundation of the permissive view.

**2. Rambam.** In [Mishneh Torah, Forbidden Intercourse 21:9], as I recall it, a man may have relations with his wife however he wishes, and may kiss any part of her body. He adds that it is nevertheless pious conduct not to deviate from the usual way, and to sanctify oneself in the act. He also forbids wasting seed.

**3. Shulchan Arukh and Rema.** In [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25:2], the Mechaber (followed by Sephardim) follows the Rambam's permissive line. He too forbids emission of seed in vain. The Rema's gloss (followed by Ashkenazim) brings the stricter approach. Check the text itself to see which words are the Mechaber's and which are the Rema's.

## Where the disagreement lies
- **Permissive view:** Some Rishonim and Acharonim read the Talmud's "whatever he wishes" literally. If it is not done to waste seed, they say it is not a Torah prohibition. Some poskim allow it only if it is done occasionally and without any emission there.
- **Restrictive view:** Others say that the usual outcome of this act is emission of seed in vain, which is a severe prohibition. Some say it is permitted only if the man withdraws before emission and completes the act naturally. Some reject even that, because it risks the prohibition. The Kabbalistic tradition (the Zohar and later sources) is very strict about wasting seed.
- **Practice:** Ashkenazi and Sephardi poskim are not neatly divided. Which authority a couple follows matters more than their community label. Many contemporary rabbis counsel against it.

## Practical notes
- Consent and mutual respect are essential. Halacha also forbids a husband from forcing his wife [Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 25].
- Physical safety matters too, since there are health risks. The Torah's concern for health applies here as well.
- It is best to ask a rabbi who handles marital questions. Many communities have rabbis or *yoatzot halacha* (women trained in family-related halacha) for these questions.

**Please consult your rabbi** for your own situation. He can ask follow-up questions and give a ruling according to your community's practice.

**Short answer:** Generally no. If you slept in your *tallit katan* (small four-cornered fringed garment), the usual Ashkenazi practice is not to make a blessing on it in the morning. Instead, you have it in mind when you bless on your *tallit gadol* (large tallit). Sephardi and Chabad practice may differ, as explained below, so check with your rabbi. I did not retrieve every source on this, so I flag where I'm less certain.

## Key Takeaways
- Putting on a garment of tzitzit normally calls for a blessing, but a garment worn continuously through the night is a special case.
- For Ashkenazim, the *Mishnah Berurah* says not to bless on a tallit katan one slept in.
- The accepted Ashkenazi practice is to bless on the tallit gadol and have the tallit katan in mind.
- Anyone who wears only a tallit katan should ask their rabbi what to do.

## The sources

**The basic rule of re-blessing.** [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 8:14] deals with someone who takes off his tallit and puts it back on. The Mechaber says he must bless again, even if he meant to put it back on right away. The Rema adds that some say no new blessing is needed if he meant to put it back on. Others say this applies specifically when a tallit katan stays on him. The Rema says this is the custom.

That passage is about taking a garment off. It does not directly address sleeping in the garment. For the Rema, the tallit katan staying on him means no re-blessing.

**The *Mishnah Berurah* on this exact case.** [Mishnah Berurah 8:24] says the custom today is to bless on the tallit gadol and have in mind to cover the tallit katan. The text continues: "ויכוין לפטור". He says this is better than the practice of blessing on the tallit katan and then immediately on the tallit gadol, because that makes a blessing that isn't needed.

He then lists cases where it isn't proper to bless on the tallit katan, even if a long time passes before the tallit gadol. One of them is "דהוא ישן בו בלילה", meaning he slept in it at night. The others are that it isn't open on most of its length, or that it is smaller than the minimum size. He refers to his comments on siman 16, which I did not retrieve.

## Practice by community
- **Ashkenazi:** Follow the *Mishnah Berurah*. No blessing on a tallit katan slept in. Bless on the tallit gadol with intent to cover the tallit katan.
- **Sephardi:** The Mechaber (8:14) is stricter about re-blessing after taking a garment off. That applies when he takes it off, not when he sleeps in it. I'm not sure of the details in Rav Ovadia Yosef and the *Ben Ish Chai* on sleeping in tzitzit, so ask a Sephardi rabbi.
- **Chabad:** I did not retrieve the *Shulchan Arukh HaRav* on this, so I can't state its position.

If you wear only a tallit katan, the cases above suggest the practice may differ. Some people take it off and put it on again with a blessing. This is a case to put to your rabbi.

Please consult your rabbi for your personal practice.

answer:
I don't know of one universal formula. The usual practice is to write your name with a short phrase acknowledging that the book is a loan from God. I'm giving these from general knowledge and didn't look them up, so treat the wording as examples.

**Key Takeaways**
- There is no single required text, so this is custom and not halacha.
- The usual inscription is "This book belongs to…" with a phrase such as "בחסדי ה'" (*b'chasdei Hashem*, "by God's kindness").
- The idea behind these phrases is that everything is God's and we are only stewards.
- Many people also add a request that the book be returned if lost.

**Common practices**
- **Name plus ownership wording.** Examples are "שייך ל…" ("belongs to…") or "ספר זה שייך ל…". Some add "בס"ד" at the top.
- **Wording that acknowledges the Owner.** Some write "קניתי בחסדי ה'" ("I acquired this through God's kindness"). Others write "ה' נתן" ("God gave"), after Job 1:21.
- **A return request.** Many write "אם נמצא, נא להחזיר ל…" ("if found, please return to…"). This is partly because returning a lost object is itself a mitzvah (Deuteronomy 22:1–3).
- **Older manuscripts and printed books.** Owners often wrote their name together with a blessing or a curse on anyone who stole the book. These inscriptions are a good example of the custom, but they are not an ideal model for today.

**The source of the idea**
- "לה' הארץ ומלואה" ("The earth is the Lord's and all it contains," Psalms 24:1). Our possessions are on loan to us.
- Pirkei Avot 3:7 puts it this way: "תן לו משלו, שאתה ושלך שלו" ("Give Him what is His, for you and what is yours are His"). This is the ownership theme you describe, and I think it is the likely source of such inscriptions.
- Halacha still treats ownership as real. Human beings can acquire things, and stealing or borrowing without permission is forbidden. Writing your name is therefore practical. It also expresses that we hold things as stewards and not as ultimate owners.
- The books themselves (*sefarim*) carry the laws of respect. One doesn't put them on the floor, and one keeps them in good condition.

answer:
The egg is a food of mourning. The ashes are a separate custom that symbolizes grief and destruction. Together they turn the last meal before the fast into a mourner's meal. Neither is a Talmudic requirement, and the reasons below are the traditional explanations rather than one fixed ruling.

## Key Takeaways
- Eggs, and lentils too, are customary mourners' foods. They are the food of the *se'udat havra'ah* (the meal of consolation) after a burial.
- Ashes are a classic sign of mourning and repentance. Dipping the egg in them makes the meal one of grief.
- The round shape of the egg and lentils is linked to the "cycle" of life and loss.
- The Rema also gives a second reason for the egg. It is tied to the fact that Israel's suffering and exile have made it "harder" and stronger, like a hard-boiled egg.
- Practice varies by community.

## The source of the custom
The Shulchan Arukh rules: "We customarily eat lentils with cooked eggs in them that are the food of mourners." The Rema adds: "There are those that are accustomed to eat hardboiled eggs that are also a food of mourners" [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 552:5]. The Rema's gloss is the basis of the Ashkenazi custom of the hard-boiled egg. The Mechaber's version has lentils with eggs.

The Mishnah describes the final meal before Tisha B'Av as one of restraint. It allows no more than a single cooked dish, no meat or wine, and no gathering of friends [Mishnah Taanit 4:7]. The egg fits that mood.

## What it represents
- **Mourning food.** The Talmud (Bava Batra 16b) connects lentils and eggs with mourners, and the Rema calls the egg a mourner's food. On Tisha B'Av we are mourners for the Temple, so we eat as mourners do before the fast begins.
- **Roundness.** A common explanation is that the egg and lentil are round, like a wheel. Mourning "rolls around" the world, and death and loss come to everyone in turn. The Midrash makes the same point about the lentil, and it is the usual explanation for the egg too.
- **No opening.** An egg has no mouth, like a mourner who is silent. Mourners are silent, and so is one who has nothing to say in the face of destruction.
- **Ashes.** Ashes are the biblical sign of mourning and repentance. See Esther 4:1, Jonah 3:6, and Daniel 9:3. The Rema records the custom of dipping the egg in ashes, or sprinkling ashes on it, to make that grief visible. The Mishnah Berurah comments on this in the same siman.
- **Resilience.** Some explain that, unlike other foods that soften when cooked, an egg gets harder the longer it is boiled. That symbolizes a people that grows stronger through suffering and exile. This is a homiletic explanation and not the main reason.

## Practice by community
- **Ashkenazi.** The usual practice is a hard-boiled egg, often with ashes, plus bread, eaten while sitting on the floor. This follows the Rema.
- **Sephardi.** The Mechaber's lentils with egg is the base text. Many Sephardim eat lentils or other simple dishes.
- **Chabad.** Chabad follows the Ashkenazi practice, with the egg and ashes, as in the Shulchan Aruch HaRav. I did not retrieve that text here, so check it directly.

The details, such as how much ash to use and whether to eat it at all, vary by custom. Consult your rabbi for your own practice.

answer:
**Short answer:** It depends on the kind of cookie and on your community's practice. Many authorities hold that ordinary cookies and cakes, which are eaten as a snack or dessert, are not subject to the *pas Yisrael* rules. Others are stringent where the item is substantial or could replace bread. Commercial cookies with reliable kosher certification are widely eaten even by people who are careful about *pas Yisrael*.

## Key Takeaways
- *Pas Yisrael* is a rabbinic decree against bread baked by a non-Jew, mainly to limit social contact that could lead to intermarriage.
- The decree is aimed at bread-like products, so cake and cookies that aren't normally eaten as a meal are often treated more leniently.
- Commercial baked goods (*pas palter*) are treated more leniently than a non-Jew's home-baked goods (*pas baal habayit*).
- Ashkenazim, Sephardim and Chabad differ in how strictly they apply this, so ask your own rabbi.

## The basic law
The Shulchan Arukh, in the section on bread of non-Jews, rules that *pas baal habayit* (bread baked by a non-Jewish householder) is not permitted. It gives the reason as the decree's "essence": it was enacted "because of the concern of intermarriage", since eating a non-Jew's bread leads to dining at their home. [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 112:2]

For *pas palter* (bread from a commercial non-Jewish baker), the Mechaber says some places are lenient. They buy it where no Jewish baker is available, because it is a *sh'at ha-dechak* (time of pressing need). The Rema adds that some permit it even where Jewish bread is available. He also defines the terms. Bread made to sell counts as commercial bread, while a baker's bread made for his own household counts as *baal habayit* bread. [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 112:2]

## Why cookies are a separate question
The decree covers *pat*, meaning bread-type baked goods made from the five grains. Poskim therefore ask whether a cookie or cake is "bread" for this purpose. My summary of the main views, from memory and not retrieved here, is:

- **Lenient view:** Items normally eaten as a snack or dessert and not as a meal substitute are not subject to the decree. The social-mingling concern is weaker for them.
- **Stringent view:** Some poskim apply the decree to any baked grain product, especially a substantial item. Some also take a stricter line on certain products, such as filled or large baked goods.

## Practice by community
- **Ashkenazi:** Practice follows the Rema and later authorities such as the Mishnah Berurah. Most Ashkenazim rely on the commercial-bakery (*pas palter*) leniency when there is reliable kosher supervision. Many are lenient on cookies. Those who keep *pas Yisrael* strictly during the Ten Days of Repentance, or year-round, often include baked goods as well.
- **Sephardi:** Practice follows the Mechaber as explained by Rav Ovadia Yosef and the Ben Ish Chai. Sephardim tend to keep *pas Yisrael* as a standard or a hiddur. Many apply it to bread but allow mezonot-type cakes and cookies. I haven't retrieved their rulings here, so please verify with a Sephardi rabbi.
- **Chabad:** Chabad generally follows the Shulchan Aruch HaRav and the Alter Rebbe's stringencies. I haven't verified how it treats cookies, so confirm with a Chabad rabbi.

## What this means in practice
- A cookie from a Jewish-owned bakery or a Jewish-owned company is *pas Yisrael* and raises no question.
- A packaged cookie from a non-Jewish company with a reliable *hechsher* is usually treated as *pas palter*. Many people eat it without concern.
- Home-baked cookies from a non-Jewish household are the most problematic case, and the Shulchan Arukh specifically does not permit *pas baal habayit*.
- A separate point: during the Ten Days of Repentance, some people are stricter than usual about *pas Yisrael*.

Because practice varies by community and by product, please consult your rabbi about your own situation.

answer:
Flight time doesn't change the halacha. The rule doesn't depend on how hard the journey is. It depends on a person's status, which is tied to where his home is. The poskim do disagree about what a visitor should do in practice, but the debate is about the visitor's status, not about whether the trip is easy.

## Key Takeaways
- Yom Tov Sheni is a rule about *where you are from* (your *makom*, or locale), not about travel difficulty or communication.
- Mainstream Ashkenazi practice is that a visitor from the Diaspora keeps one day in private, as in his home community. Many Sephardi poskim, and Chabad, differ in some details.
- Flight time is irrelevant, because the custom was kept even when messengers from Israel took months, and because it was explicitly kept after the calendar became known.
- The modern debate is about visitors who intend to stay, not about travel speed.

## Why speed doesn't change the law
The origin of the second day was doubt about the date of Rosh Chodesh, since messengers from the *Beit Din* in Israel might not arrive in time. The Talmud says that once the calendar was fixed (under Hillel II), the Diaspora still had to keep the second day. The reason was a "custom of your ancestors," and a concern that persecution might return and the calendar knowledge be forgotten ([Beitzah 4b](https://www.sefaria.org/Beitzah.4b)). Rambam rules the same way. So the day has long been a *minhag avoteinu* (ancestral custom) that carries the force of a binding takkanah, and it no longer depends on the original doubt. Modern communication therefore doesn't affect it. It was already irrelevant a thousand years ago.

## What the visitor actually does
The rule for visitors is a separate question, and it also depends on the person's status. Note that [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 496:3](https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh,_Orach_Chayim.496.3) covers the *reverse* case, Israelis in the Diaspora. They are bound by the local second day if they have reached a settled place, even if they intend to return. That shows the law is tied to where you are, not to how long you've been traveling.

For a Diaspora resident visiting Israel, the main views are:
- **Ashkenazi, mainstream:** he keeps Yom Tov Sheni as a Diaspora resident. In practice he avoids *melacha* (work) in public and does not make it obvious. The accepted approach is to keep the second day as a private Yom Tov in his own home. He also respects Israeli practice, so he does not do things in front of locals that would cause a *chillul Yom Tov* for them. This follows the Chacham Tzvi and the Mishnah Berurah.
- **Sephardi:** Rav Ovadia Yosef generally ruled that a visitor in Israel keeps the second day as a Diaspora resident would, again privately.
- **Chabad:** a visitor who intends to return follows his home practice and keeps two days, though Chabad has specific rulings on what he may do and on prayer. Check with a Chabad rav.
- **Minority view:** some poskim hold that someone who plans to settle or who has "made himself an Israeli" in practice keeps one day. That is a question of his own status, not of how easy the flight was.

## What is changing
The practical difficulty is real. Visitors often can't cook, use electricity or do their normal Yom Tov things while everyone around them is keeping a weekday. That is why poskim have given guidance on what is permitted privately, such as continuing to light candles, making *Kiddush* for oneself, and eating in a sukkah. This is a question of how to apply the law, and it doesn't change the law. Some contemporary poskim have written on cases such as a *yeshiva* student who spends the year in Israel, or someone who flies in just for the holiday.

Consult your rabbi for your personal situation, especially if you are staying in Israel for an extended period or considering *aliyah*.

answer:
**Short answer:** I don't think this reasoning works, and it is not a safe basis for skipping *tevilah* (immersion of a new vessel). Once the lid has been bought from a non-Jew as a finished, usable vessel, the obligation is already in place. Taking it apart and reassembling it doesn't remove that obligation. Immersing the lid, which takes a minute, is the safe course.

My Sefaria lookups failed (rate-limit errors), so I didn't read the texts in this session. Below I name the sources without exact se'if numbers and rely on well-known positions. Please check them.

## Key Takeaways
- *Tevilah* applies to metal and glass eating and cooking vessels that a Jew acquires from a non-Jew. The source is [Numbers 31:23], as developed in [Avodah Zarah 75b] and [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 120].
- The status depends on the vessel being a finished vessel (*gmar melacha*, completed manufacture) when it leaves the non-Jew's hands. It does not depend on how well it performs.
- Adding a handle or other improvement to an already usable vessel is generally not seen as "making" the vessel. The vessel was already a vessel.
- The case where a Jew's completion exempts is different. There, the vessel was not yet a usable keli when the Jew received it, or the Jew himself manufactured it.
- If you are unsure, the usual practice is to immerse without a blessing. Consult your rabbi.

## Why the argument is shaky

**1. A lid with a hole is already a lid.** You are arguing that the lid's function is to trap steam and return it to the food, and that a hole defeats this. But a lid with a hole still covers the pot, still sits over hot food, and is still usable, just less efficiently. A vessel is "finished" when it can be used for its purpose. Better performance is an improvement, not a completion. Attaching a handle is the classic example of an improvement. Poskim distinguish between a Jew completing an unfinished item and a Jew merely improving a finished one. In the second case the vessel was already a keli when it came from the non-Jew, so it was already obligated.

**2. The hole is not what makes the lid a keli.** You say a Jew completing the vessel "defines it as a keli to begin with." The lid was a vessel when you bought it. The handle on the lid is just a handle. Nothing in your description suggests that without the handle it would be a shapeless piece of metal.

**3. You would be unscrewing it only to avoid the obligation.** A vessel that was already bound to *tevilah* does not become exempt because you dismantle it and reassemble it. The obligation attaches at the moment of acquisition. Doing this deliberately is also the kind of contrived arrangement the poskim distrust.

**4. If you did get it unassembled.** Suppose a lid was sold in pieces, with no usable lid until you put it together. Then there is a real discussion among later poskim about whether a Jew's assembly counts as the completion that exempts it. Some are lenient, others require *tevilah* anyway. The two cases are not the same, and I can't give you a clear ruling on the second one. This is a question for a rav.

## Practical bottom line
- If the lid came to you as a finished lid, immerse it. Whether to say the blessing (*al tevilat keli*) depends on whether the lid is considered a full keli and on your community's practice. For a real doubt, the usual approach is to immerse without a blessing.
- If you want to rely on the argument that your assembly completes the vessel, bring the actual lid and its history to your rabbi. Say whether you bought it assembled or in parts, what the lid is made of, and whether it touches the food.

This is not a final ruling for your situation, so please consult your rabbi.

answer:
**Short answer:** Gambling for money, such as dice, cards or betting, is forbidden or strongly discouraged in the classic sources. Raffles are treated differently, and many authorities permit them in certain forms, especially charity raffles. The details depend on the type of raffle and on your community's practice.

## Key Takeaways
- The Mishnah disqualifies a dice-gambler from serving as a witness or judge [Sanhedrin 24b].
- The Talmud gives two reasons: the winnings aren't a real, binding transfer (*asmakhta*), or gambling is not "settling the world" (*yishuvo shel olam*).
- Rambam treats gambling as rabbinic-level "robbery" [Mishneh Torah, Robbery and Lost Property 6:10].
- The Rema says the custom spread to be lenient, and only someone with no other livelihood is disqualified [Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat 370:3].
- Raffles are a separate question, and many poskim permit them, especially for charity.

## The source: the dice-player (*mesachek bekuvya*)
The Mishnah lists those disqualified from testimony: "הַמְשַׂחֵק בְּקוּבְיָא" ("one who plays with dice"), along with usurers, pigeon-racers and traders in Shemitah produce [Sanhedrin 24b].

The Gemara gives two explanations:
- **Rami bar Chama:** the bet is an *asmakhta*, meaning a commitment made without real finality. The loser never fully intends to hand over the money, so the winner takes it without a valid transfer.
- **Rav Sheshet:** the gambler is "not engaged in the settlement of the world," meaning he contributes nothing productive.

The practical difference is a gambler who also has another trade. Rav Sheshet's reason, backed by Rabbi Yehudah in the Mishnah, disqualifies only someone whose sole occupation is gambling.

## The codes
- **Rambam** describes gambling with dice, pebbles, or racing animals. He rules: "הֲרֵי זֶה גֵּזֶל מִדִּבְרֵיהֶם". ("This is robbery according to Rabbinic decree.") This applies even though the loser consents, because the winner takes money "for nothing, as part of the frivolous sport" [Mishneh Torah, Robbery and Lost Property 6:10]. He rules that all forms of gambling are forbidden.
- **Shulchan Arukh (Mechaber):** he cites one view that gambling with a non-Jew is not robbery but is still forbidden as "דְּבָרִים בְּטֵלִים" (idle matters). A person should spend his life on wisdom and on the settlement of the world. He then cites a view that the gambler is disqualified only if he has no other trade [Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat 370:3].
- **Rema (the gloss beginning *Hagah*, followed by Ashkenazim):** he writes that the custom has spread to follow the lenient view, to play with dice. Only someone with no other occupation is disqualified [Shulchan Arukh, Choshen Mishpat 370:3].

Ashkenazi and Sephardi practice therefore differ in emphasis, but in practice most poskim of all communities discourage regular gambling. The reasons are *bittul Torah* (wasting time that should go to Torah study), the risk of addiction, and the problem of *asmakhta*. Rav Ovadia Yosef and the Mishnah Berurah both discourage it. I did not retrieve their exact wording here, so I am not quoting them.

## Raffles and lotteries
I did not retrieve a specific source on raffles, so this part is a summary of the general positions rather than a citation-backed ruling.

- **Charity raffles:** many poskim permit them. The ticket is seen as a donation, and the prize is a gift from the organizers. No participant loses money to another participant, so the *asmakhta* and "robbery" concerns do not apply in the same way.
- **Private or commercial raffles:** here participants pay into a pool that others win. Poskim are more divided. Some treat it like gambling, and others permit it when the rules are clear and everyone agrees in advance.
- **State lotteries and casinos:** these are generally discouraged. Many authorities see a real gambling problem, as well as *bittul Torah* and the risk of addiction. Some are more lenient on a small, occasional lottery ticket.
- **Games for fun:** playing cards or games without money, or for tiny stakes, is generally not a problem. Some poskim are strict even about those on Shabbat or during Torah-study time.

## Practical bottom line
Regular gambling is forbidden for those who rely on it for income, and it is strongly discouraged for everyone. A charity raffle is the most widely accepted case. For a specific raffle, lottery or game, ask your rabbi, since the answer depends on how it is structured.

**Short answer:** I can't confirm it. People often say that attending a *pidyon haben* (redemption of the firstborn son) is worth 80 fasts, but I couldn't find that statement in the Talmud or the Shulchan Arukh. Treat it as a popular saying, not an established halachic fact. The attribution I've heard (that the saying goes back to a kabbalistic or later source) is something I couldn't verify, so I won't name one.

## Key Takeaways
- I found no source for "80 fasts" in the codes or the Talmud.
- The seudah (festive meal) at a pidyon haben is a real *seudat mitzvah* (a meal connected to a mitzvah), and it is a custom with early roots.
- Joining a mitzvah celebration is meritorious, but no one can calculate its reward as a number of fasts.

## What the sources do say
- **The mitzvah:** The father must redeem his firstborn son from a Kohen for five *selaim* (silver coins), based on [Numbers 18:15-16].
- **The meal:** The Rema records that "some write that it is customary to make a seudah at the time of the redemption." The Hebrew is "ויש שכתבו שנהגו לעשות סעודה בשעת הפדיון" [Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 305:10]. This is the Rema's gloss, so it is the Ashkenazi source. It says the meal is a custom. It says nothing about fasts.
- **The wine:** The Kohen also makes a blessing on wine right after the redemption "to publicize the matter" (*lefarsumei milta*). The same gloss says this.

## How to think about the "80 fasts"
- A seudat mitzvah has real value. Attending, rejoicing with the family, and eating there all count as taking part in a mitzvah.
- The "80 fasts" figure is probably a way of saying that this participation carries great merit. It is not a measured halachic equivalence, and no one needs to treat it as literal.
- If you want to cite it, say "it's said that…". Don't present it as halacha.
- It also does not mean you can skip a fast you are obligated to keep. A pidyon haben does not replace a communal fast, for example.

If you remember where you heard it, tell me. I can check that source. For a practical question, such as attending on a fast day, ask your rabbi.

answer:
Simchat Torah, as a named holiday with its own celebrations, is indeed later than the Torah and the Talmud. Its two roots are older, though. One is the Biblical festival of Shemini Atzeret. The other is the Talmudic practice of reading the last portion of the Torah on the day after it. The name and most of the dancing customs developed in the Geonic and medieval periods.

## Key Takeaways
- Shemini Atzeret is the Biblical holiday, and the Torah never mentions Simchat Torah.
- The Talmud already records reading *Vezot HaBerakhah* (the last portion of the Torah) on the second day in the Diaspora, so the completion of the Torah on this date is ancient.
- The name "Simchat Torah" and the festive meal come from later custom, which the Rema records.
- Hakafot (the Torah-scroll processions) and the calling up of all the children are later customs, and each community keeps its own version.
- In Israel, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah fall on the same day. In the Diaspora they are two days.

## The Biblical base: Shemini Atzeret
The Torah commands an "eighth day" of assembly after Sukkot (Leviticus 23:36). It is a separate festival with no *lulav* and no *sukkah* obligation. Nothing in the Torah mentions completing the Torah reading.

## The Talmudic stage
The Gemara in [Megillah 31a](https://www.sefaria.org/Megillah.31a) lists the readings for each festival. For the last day of the festival it says:
"יוֹם טוֹב הָאַחֲרוֹן קוֹרִין ״כׇּל הַבְּכוֹר״ ... לְמָחָר קוֹרִין ״וְזֹאת הַבְּרָכָה״, וּמַפְטִירִין ״וַיַּעֲמֹד שְׁלֹמֹה״"
("On the last Yom Tov they read 'All the firstborn'... The next day they read 'And this is the blessing,' and the haftarah is 'And Solomon stood.'")

So the Babylonian communities finished the Torah on the day after Shemini Atzeret. That is the core of the holiday. The Gemara gives it no special name and mentions no dancing. The practice also reflects the Babylonian annual reading cycle. The Land of Israel followed a roughly three-year cycle at the time, and the annual cycle later became universal.

## The medieval development
- **The name.** The Rema's gloss to [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 669:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh,_Orach_Chayim.669.1) says: "וקורין י"ט האחרון שמחת תורה לפי ששמחין ועושין בו סעודת משתה לגמרה של תורה" ("The last Yom Tov is called Simchat Torah because we rejoice and hold a festive meal for the completion of the Torah"). I recall that the name appears in Geonic-era and later medieval sources, but I did not look up the earliest instance.
- **Donations and a feast.** The Rema, citing the Tur, says the one who completes the Torah and the one who begins Genesis pledge donations and invite others to a feast. In Ashkenazi communities these two are the *Chatan Torah* and *Chatan Bereishit* ("bridegroom" of the Torah and of Genesis).
- **Taking out all the scrolls.** The Rema notes the custom "in these countries" to take out every scroll from the ark at night and in the morning and to sing hymns.
- **Hakafot.** The Rema says: "נהגו להקיף עם ספרי התורה הבימה ... כמו שמקיפים עם הלולב" ("They circle the bimah with Torah scrolls, as one circles with the *lulav*"). He adds that "all of this is out of joy."
- **Many readers.** The Rema records calling many people to the Torah and repeating a section, and calling up all the children to hear "the angel who redeemed me" (Genesis 48:16). He says there is "no prohibition" in repeating readings. He also records the custom of letting even a child complete the Torah.

Many sources attribute the spread of the elaborate dancing and the evening Hakafot to the 16th-century Safed kabbalists. I'm giving that from memory and have not verified it here.

## The reading on the day
According to the Rema's text on [Orach Chayim 669:1](https://www.sefaria.org/Shulchan_Arukh,_Orach_Chayim.669.1), the Torah reading goes as follows:
- From the first scroll we read *Vezot HaBerakhah* to the end of the Torah.
- From the second we read Genesis 1:1–2:3.
- From the third, the *maftir*, we read the festival portion.
- The haftarah is Joshua 1:1 ("After the death of Moses").

The Torah ends and begins again at once, which expresses that the Torah is never "finished."

## Community differences
- **Israel:** Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah are one day.
- **Diaspora:** They are two days. Simchat Torah is the second day.
- **Ashkenazi and Sephardi:** The customs in the Rema's gloss are the Ashkenazi ones. Sephardi and Eastern communities also dance with the scrolls, but they differ in details such as the timing of Hakafot, the readings, and the honors, so each community follows its own tradition. I did not retrieve Sephardi sources here.
- **Chabad:** Chabad is known for extended Hakafot and distinctive customs. I did not verify these here.

If you want to practice any of these customs yourself, ask your rabbi what your community does.

I can also look at the Torah-reading honors or the Hakafot customs in more detail if you'd like.

I don't know of any prohibition, disapproval, or required practice about height in the Talmud or the codes. If you saw a specific claim, tell me where, and I'll check it.

**Key Takeaways**
- I know of no halachic rule, positive or negative, about the relative height of spouses.
- The Talmud's advice on compatibility is about age and temperament, not height.
- Rabbinic literature stresses honoring one's wife, which doesn't depend on height.
- Modern popular claims about height usually have no textual source.

## What the sources do address

**Suitability in marriage.** [Yevamot 44a] says the elders "advise him what is fitting for him." If he is young and she old, or he old and she young, they tell him: "כְּלָךְ אֵצֶל שֶׁכְּמוֹתְךָ, וְאַל תָּשִׂים קְטָטָה בְּבֵיתֶךָ" ("Go to one like yourself, and don't place strife in your home"). This is the closest Talmudic idea to your question. The concern is *shalom bayit* (peace in the home). The example given is age, and the passage says nothing about height. It is also advice, not a legal requirement.

**Honoring one's wife.** [Bava Metzia 59a] teaches that a man should take care to honor his wife, because blessing in the home comes through her. I'm citing this from memory and didn't retrieve it in this session, so check the wording yourself. Nothing there makes her honor or his standing depend on physical size.

**"Ezer kenegdo."** Genesis 2:18 describes the wife as a helper "opposite him" (*ezer kenegdo*). [Yevamot 63a] reads this as "if he merits, a help; if not, against him." That is about the quality of the relationship, not stature.

## Practical bottom line
Halachically, height plays no role in the validity of a marriage, in *kiddushin* (betrothal), or in the couple's obligations. The sources point to character, compatibility, mutual respect, and *shalom bayit* as what matters. answer:
**Yes, you can still put on tefillin. The time for the mitzvah lasts until sunset, so at 5 pm you have time. Put them on first and then pray Mincha while wearing them.**

I couldn't pull exact zmanim, so please check a local calendar for today's sunset in Mexico City. In late November it is roughly 5:40–5:50 pm, which is not much time. Don't delay.

## Key Takeaways
- Tefillin may be worn any time during the day, until sunset.
- Put them on before Mincha, so they are on during the Amidah.
- Make the blessing as usual, if you are clearly before sunset.
- If you also missed Shacharit, pray a second Amidah after Mincha as a makeup prayer.
- Don't put them on at twilight (*bein hashmashot*, the period after sunset).

## Why you can still do it
The Shulchan Arukh says: "מצותן להיותם עליו כל היום", meaning "It is a mitzvah to have them on all day" [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 37:2]. We usually don't keep them on all day because they require a clean body and sustained focus. The same se'if adds that a person must make sure they are on during the Shema and the Amidah. The Shulchan Arukh's rule on when tefillin may be worn (Orach Chayim 30) runs from dawn until sunset. I couldn't retrieve that text just now, so I am citing it from memory.

## The order
1. **Put on tefillin**, hand first and then head, with the usual blessings. The standard practice is to make the blessing in the afternoon too, because the mitzvah applies all day. If you are unsure, or it is already close to sunset, ask your rabbi.
2. **Pray Mincha with the tefillin on.** This fulfills the requirement that they be on during the Amidah [Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 37:2].
3. **Remove them** after Mincha. Don't leave them on past sunset.

## If you also missed Shacharit
- You can't make up the morning Shema or the morning blessings of the Shema.
- If you missed the Shacharit Amidah, the usual rule is to pray Mincha first and then a second Amidah, which makes up the missed prayer. Doing it in this order is the standard approach. Do it with tefillin on as well.
- The Ashkenazi, Sephardi and Chabad practices are the same on the basic points here. Details such as additions to the second Amidah can differ.

Please consult your rabbi for your own situation, especially if sunset is close.
